st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s task-level, work-redesign framing and adds historical evidence on labour adjustment: automation severely displaced incumbent workers while later cohorts were absorbed through occupational reallocation and organisational creation of new work. It materially extends the synthesis by showing that adjustment varies with worker-specific human capital and aggregate demand, while appropriately limiting direct generalisation to modern legal AI.
qs: Similar to Humlum (2021), our results suggest these effects exist on a continuum: incum- bent workers with the least time to adjust (and most invested in the occupation) suffer the largest consequences, whereas future generations are better able to adapt.

st.t: Worker exposure: Technical susceptibility differs from displacement
st.an: The source materially develops the cluster’s distinction between technological susceptibility and realised displacement by supplying historical evidence of heterogeneous adjustment: telephone cutovers reduced operator persistence and overall employment, especially among older incumbents, while also increasing geographic mobility. It supports uneven rather than frictionless adjustment, without claiming that these historical effects forecast contemporary AI displacement.

st.t: Automation adjustment: Later employment hides incumbent losses
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: telephone automation left employment rates intact for later cohorts while causing persistent employment and career-quality losses for incumbent operators. It also supports the cluster’s qualifications that replacement work varied in quality, adjustment likely depended on new labor demand, and this historical case should not be treated as a universal AI forecast.
qs: Our exercise comprises two distinct but closely related analyses, on two samples, answering two questions: (i) how did automating telephone service affect incumbent tele- phone operators and (ii) how did it affect future generations of young women entering the labor market?

Taken                                                   1 ^Ltogether, these results suggest that although existing workers may be exposed to job loss, local economies can adjust to large automation shocks over medium horizons.

st.t: Cohort employment: Stable totals conceal occupational downgrading
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition. It distinguishes substantial, lasting employment and occupational losses among incumbent telephone operators from near-zero overall employment effects in successive cohorts of young women, while documenting occupational reallocation and modest downgrading within those cohorts. Its historical scope and methodological qualifications limit extrapolation but do not undermine the proposition.

st.t: Historical automation: Occupational loss differs from unemployment
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central distinction: telephone automation sharply reduced operator employment without a detectable decline in overall employment among successive young-women cohorts, while incumbent operators experienced persistent employment losses and occupational downgrading. Its robustness checks strengthen that pattern but retain pretrend, precision, mechanism and generalizability limits.

st.t: Job exposure: Which tasks vanish changes outcomes
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s distinction between automation-driven job loss and uncertain net employment outcomes. Its historical evidence leaves the emergence of replacement work unresolved and finds no spillovers into the particular substitute occupations examined, reinforcing the need to avoid inferring economy-wide displacement or adjustment from task automation alone.
qs: As a result, questions such as whether, when, and how new work will materialize to offset the jobs lost to automation are not fully resolved.
However, we do not see evidence of spillovers: wages did not fall in substitute occupations, and young white women’s share of these jobs did not grow.

st.t: Worker displacement: Aggregate recovery masks career damage
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal distinction: telephone automation caused lasting career and employment losses for incumbent operators, while later cohorts experienced no detectable decline in overall employment. It also supports the cluster’s qualifications concerning occupational downgrading, uneven age effects, incomplete adjustment mechanisms and limited generalisability.

kp.k: Automation harmed incumbents more than future entrants
kp.d: Feigenbaum and Gross study telephone automation using 1910–1940 census data and local adoption timing. Their central finding distinguishes displaced incumbent operators, who experienced persistent employment and occupational losses, from subsequent cohorts of young women, whose overall employment rates did not decline. This is historical evidence about telephone operation, not a direct finding about AI or legal employment.
qs: Using a new genealogy-based census-linking method, we show that incumbent telephone operators were most impacted, and a decade later more likely to be in lower-paying occupations or no longer working.
By contrast, the shock did not reduce future cohorts’ employment rates.

kp.k: Mechanical switching sharply reduced entry-level operator opportunities
kp.d: The authors report an immediate, permanent 50–80% decline in young operators after local cutovers, eliminating around 2% of the focal group's jobs. High turnover meant the loss of entry-level opportunities potentially affected substantially more women than the employment share suggests. Bell telephones on dial increased to 32% by 1930 and 60% by 1940, although complete network diffusion took until 1978.
qs: Around 2% of this group’s jobs were permanently replaced by machines overnight, one city at a time.

These jobs comprised around 2% of employment for this group, and even more for those under age 20—and given turnover rates, this shock may have foreclosed entry-level job opportunities for as much as 10 to 15% of peak cohorts.

kp.k: Automation selectively replaced tasks, ages, and genders
kp.d: Mechanical switching replaced local call connection rather than all telephone work. Operators remained necessary for long-distance calls, information, emergencies, and remaining manual subscribers. These residual tasks favored experienced, generally older operators; equipment maintenance created demand for technicians who were generally men. The authors therefore characterize the change as skill-, age-, and gender-biased.
qs: Mechanical switching specifically replaced operators in connecting local calls, and AT&T records from the 1910s projected that the automatic equipment would reduce the number of operators in large cities by up to 70 to 80% (Gherardi 1917).
Because these were more complex tasks, the residual operating needs required better trained, more experienced operators, who tended to be older.
Automatic switching also increased demand for technicians to maintain the automatic equipment, who tended to be men.

kp.d: Drawing on company records, related research, and regressions, the authors argue that growing network complexity and the cost of manual switching primarily drove automation. City population explains adoption much more strongly than measured labor-market characteristics. Preparations typically lasted 2–3 years, but actual cutovers took minutes; local operating-company managers determined timing.
qs: Drawing on company records and empirical evidence, we find that automation was primarily a response to the technical demands of the growing telephone network, rather than labor market conditions.
Mechanization was an effort to slow this cost growth and support the firm’s continued expansion.

kp.k: Research separates incumbent trajectories from cohort adjustment
kp.d: The core city-age panel analysis covers 2,845 cities with populations no greater than 100,000 in 1920, including 261 with cutovers before 1940. It uses staggered event studies and difference-in-differences with fixed effects, population controls, and city-clustered standard errors. A separate incumbent analysis compares operators with demographically matched working women in their neighborhoods and operators in untreated cities. The authors report robustness to alternative event-study estimators, continuous newspaper coverage, expected employment-growth controls, and a large-city long-differences design.
qs: In all of our analyses, our focus will be on cities with population ≤100,000 in 1920, where automation was typically a discrete event (Appendix Figure B.2).
We cluster standard errors at the city level.

For certain analyses, we also estimate two-year intervals to better understand adjustment dynamics, with the important caveat that each bin (in event time) will contain different treated cities, since each city is measured once every ten years (and will thus be included in every fifth bin).

kp.k: Genealogical linking follows women through marriage-related name changes
kp.d: FamilySearch links address a limitation of conventional historical census matching: women's surname changes after marriage. The procedure yields 16,253 operators linked from 1920 to 1930 and 11,220 from 1930 to 1940, with approximately 4.7 linked control women per operator. The authors acknowledge nonrandom genealogical coverage, use inverse propensity weights for observable selection, and report that cutovers do not significantly predict linking.
qs: This process yields a sample of 16,253 operators linked from 1920 to 1930 and another 11,220 linked from 1930 to 1940, the latter number lower because we exclude operators in cities already cutover to dial.
The set of operators in this sample is inevitably not random.
To account for this bias, we follow Bailey et al. (2020) and construct inverse propensity weights (IPW).

kp.k: Older incumbents experienced the largest employment losses
kp.d: Tables IV and V estimate that exposed incumbent operators were 8.1–8.7 percentage points less likely to remain telephone-industry operators a decade later and 3.6–4.2 points less likely to be working. For those initially aged 26+, the employment decline was 6.6–7.5 points; younger workers' employment effects were generally smaller and less precise. Other telephone-industry jobs or private-switchboard positions absorbed only a small fraction of displaced operators.
qs: This effect shaves roughly one-third off of the base rate at which these women continued working as telephone operators in non-cutover cities, relative to their matched controls.
The cutover effects are largest for women aged 26+, the set of operators who were most likely to remain employed as operators without a cutover.
Former telephone operators were very unlikely to do either, independent of cutovers or as a result of them (Table IV, Panels B and C).

kp.k: Continuing incumbents experienced occupational downgrading and migration
kp.d: Among incumbents still working, Table VI estimates an approximately 11-percentage-point reduction in remaining in the same occupation and industry, a −0.056 effect on log occupation score, and an approximately 10-percentage-point increase in declining occupation-score decile. Occupation scores proxy earnings using female occupational median incomes in 1940; they do not measure individual wage changes. Migration also increased, particularly among older incumbents, although some estimates are imprecise.
qs: In Table VI, we find that operators who continued working were roughly 11 p.p. (or early 40%) more likely than their peers to switch careers, and suggestive evidence that their new occupations were lower status after automation.
Across all measures, we find increased migration of incumbent operators after cutovers, with these effects are driven by older incumbents (ages 21-25 or 26+).

kp.d: For white, American-born women aged 16–25, Table VII estimates a −0.66-percentage-point change in operator employment as a share of the population but a statistically insignificant +0.03-point change in overall employment. Conditional on working, Table VIII estimates a −1.51-point operator share, +0.52-point typist/secretarial share, and +0.81-point restaurant-work share. Younger women disproportionately entered lower-paying service work; older young women more often entered similar-paying secretarial work. Average log occupation score fell 0.010 overall and 0.019 among ages 16–20.
qs: Growth in middle-skill secretarial jobs and low-skill service jobs offset most of the operator jobs lost to automation.
We find no effects on young women’s employment rates.
We likewise find no effects on the fraction in school or married, and a modest impact on fertility for the youngest women in our sample.

kp.k: Stable measured wages do not establish unchanged earnings
kp.d: Cross-sectional 1940 census data on 1939 earnings show no systematic wage declines associated with cutovers across timing-, age-, and sex-based comparisons. However, the authors cannot statistically rule out wage changes of ±10%, lack an earlier comparable wage panel, and acknowledge that demand growth and wage declines could coexist in different occupations. Their occupational-share tests also find no evidence that young white women crowded other demographic groups out of substitute occupations.
qs: Across these tests, we do not find evidence of systematic wage declines or differences in relation to cutovers (Appendix E.1.1).

These results should be interpreted with some caution, given standard errors (we cannot statistically rule out wage changes of ±10%), which may be due to heterogeneous effects, noise in the wage data, or more limited power afforded by a smaller set of cutovers (72 vs. the 261 in our main sample).
Reinstating demand growth and wage declines could each be present in different occupations.

kp.k: Direct productivity and complementary employment explain little adjustment
kp.d: The authors argue that maintenance and other complementary jobs were too few and predominantly male to offset young women's losses. Telephone rates typically rose rather than fell, and their back-of-the-envelope calculation estimates annual time savings of around 1.4 hours per business telephone. They also find no concurrent changes in occupations associated with electricity or automobiles, arguing against these technologies explaining the observed employment adjustment.
qs: But the employment growth in these occupations was neither large enough, nor female enough, to offset the massive loss of jobs for young women: there were only a few thousand such engineers, and essentially all were male.
We estimate these savings to have been around 1.4 hours per telephone set.
Any such productivity gains would have had to run through lower telephone service prices or higher service quality.

kp.k: New uses of existing occupations support task reinstatement
kp.d: The authors interpret their evidence as most consistent with Acemoglu and Restrepo's theory that automation encourages new uses for newly abundant labor. Their measure is new local occupation-industry pairings, not directly observed task content. Table E.7 estimates a 0.41-percentage-point increase in young women's secretarial employment in locally new industries, accounting for most of the overall secretarial increase. Organizational innovation or diffusion can therefore constitute new work without a new technology or occupation; comparable evidence is weaker for restaurant work.
qs: The Acemoglu and Restrepo (2018) mechanism is difficult to evaluate directly without measures of the specific task content of workers’ jobs.
Our focus is especially on locally-new work, and we are agnostic on whether it is a product of invention or diffusion (both would be consistent with theory).

We find significant growth in typist, stenographic, and secretarial employment in new industries, but not existing industries, with most of the effect in Table VIII attributable to new industries—consistent with the conjecture that employment in these fields was enabled by the growth of new work.

kp.d: Employment adjustment varied with local economic conditions. The authors report less favorable outcomes in manufacturing-intensive cities, where employment was predominantly male, and employment declines following cutovers in cities experiencing the most severe Great Depression contractions. They interpret these patterns as evidence that demand reinstatement is conditional rather than automatic. They find no differential effects by their measured technological conditions.
qs: We do not find differential effects across cities by technological conditions.
This suggests that aggregate demand has a direct impact on whether, when, and to what degree labor demand can recover from large automation shocks.
That the estimated effect is monotonic in depression severity bolsters this takeaway.

kp.k: Historical lessons require demographic and technological qualifications
kp.d: The authors connect age differences to occupation- and firm-specific human capital and task-skill mismatch: incumbents with greater investment and less adjustment time suffer more, while future cohorts adapt. They argue that the case offers general theoretical insights but acknowledge its smaller overall employment exposure than broad modern technologies and its distinctive gender, racial, and class setting. Young white women may have had more alternative opportunities than other women. The paper leaves automation's effects on social ties and families as research questions, not demonstrated findings.
qs: Older incumbent workers, who may have spent years building occupation- and firm-specific human capital that is suddenly obsolete, are more adversely affected.
Younger workers—including future generations not yet in the labor force, or not even yet born—are more adaptive to an evolving labor market.
Operators (and potential future operators) were not only directly exposed to automation, but may have also had access to a wider range of other work opportunities than other women.
A residual question, however, is how general historical episodes such as this one may be.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Feigenbaum and Gross find that mechanizing telephone operation eliminated a major entry-level occupation without reducing subsequent cohorts’ overall employment, while imposing lasting costs on incumbent operators.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain historical automation study, not a study of AI adoption or legal services. The authors estimate that local cutovers reduced the number of young telephone operators by 50–80%. Incumbent operators were less likely to remain employed a decade later and, conditional on working, more likely to enter lower-paying occupations. Subsequent cohorts instead found work in middle-skill clerical occupations and lower-skill services. Stable overall employment did not mean unchanged job quality: Table VIII reports a small decline in occupation scores, concentrated among the youngest women. The authors interpret expansion of secretarial employment into locally new industries as evidence consistent with countervailing demand and task reinstatement, rather than direct proof of the creation of new tasks. They do not predict a numerical employment effect for contemporary AI or the legal profession.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on archival adoption records, newspaper reports, complete-count census data, and genealogically linked individual records, analyzed using staggered adoption and matched comparisons.
pts.d: The authors combine AT&T records and a review of more than 26,000 newspaper pages with census outcomes from 1910–1940. Their main successive-cohort analysis includes 2,845 cities with populations no greater than 100,000 in 1920, including 261 with cutovers before the 1940 census. Event studies and difference-in-differences specifications include geographic and temporal fixed effects and population-related controls. Incumbent analyses link 16,253 operators from 1920 to 1930 and 11,220 from 1930 to 1940, comparing exposed operators with operators in untreated cities and demographically matched working women from their neighborhoods; inverse propensity weights address observable linking selection. In the pair-fixed-effects specifications, cutovers lower decade-later employment by 3.6 percentage points overall and 7.5 points for operators initially aged 26 or older. Among those still working, the occupation-score coefficient is −0.056 log points, and the probability of a decline in occupation-score decile rises by 10.1 percentage points. These scores proxy occupation-level earnings rather than measuring individual wage losses. Wage analyses use 1939 earnings reported in the 1940 census and find no systematic declines, but the authors explicitly acknowledge limited precision. Evidence for task reinstatement uses new local occupation–industry pairings and tests of alternative mechanisms, not direct observations of task content.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern early twentieth-century automation, with immediate occupational displacement and adjustment observed over census intervals; recovery depends on economic conditions.
pts.d: The February 2024 revision studies census outcomes from 1910–1940, focusing on the automation wave of the 1920s and 1930s. Individual outcomes are measured ten years after the baseline census, with cutovers occurring sometime in the intervening decade—not necessarily ten years before the outcome observation. Cutovers were discrete local events following two to three years of preparation, although network-wide diffusion lasted nearly sixty years. Two-year event-time bins draw on different cities because each city is observed only decennially. The authors characterize adjustment as fairly quick or occurring over medium horizons, but do not establish an exact universal recovery period. Countervailing demand was weaker in manufacturing-intensive cities and places experiencing severe Great Depression contractions. They regard the historical findings as relevant to general automation mechanisms but acknowledge differences from broad technologies such as AI, the smaller share of total employment exposed, and the distinctive social position of the women studied.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Costs fall most heavily on established operators, especially older incumbents; future entrants adapt through different occupations, with outcomes varying by age and social context.
pts.d: The focal successive-cohort population is white, American-born women aged 16–25, whose employment opportunities were especially exposed to local call-switching automation. Older incumbent operators faced larger employment losses and increased migration, consistent with greater occupation-specific investment. Among future entrants, women aged 21–25 more often entered similarly paid secretarial work, while teenagers more often entered lower-paid services such as restaurant work. Remaining operator positions involved more complex services and generally required experienced workers; maintenance jobs tended to employ men and did not replace the lost opportunities for young women. The authors find no evidence that the focal group crowded other demographic groups out of substitute occupations, while acknowledging historical racial and gender barriers. Lawyers and physicians appear only as illustrative potential employers of stenographers, not as populations for which AI effects are measured.
